title: Tracking spending
objective: Choose a tracking method and categorise a month of transactions

q.prompt: When people guess their monthly spending from memory, what do they most often leave out?

options.why: Big fixed bills are easy to remember. It's the small stuff that slips through.

options.text: Their biggest purchase of the month
options.why: Big one-offs stick in memory. Little repeats don't.

q.explanation: Coffees, delivery fees and forgotten subscriptions are easy to miss, which is why tracking beats guessing.

q.prompt: True or false: you need a paid budgeting app to track your spending properly.
q.explanation: Your banking app, a free spreadsheet or a notebook all work. The best method is the one you'll keep using.

screens.title: Pick a method you'll stick with
screens.body: Tracking means recording what you actually spend, then comparing it with your budget. Most Australian banking apps sort transactions into categories for you. A spreadsheet gives more control. Cash envelopes make limits physical. Consistency matters more than the tool.

screens.title: Use the same categories as your budget
screens.body: Pick 6 to 8 categories that match your budget lines: housing, groceries, transport, bills, eating out, fun, savings. Once a month, total each one and compare it with the plan. Overspending in one category is information, not failure.

screens.title: Worked example: Noah's first week
screens.body: Noah, 24, in Sydney, categorises a week from his statement.

screens.title: Noah's category totals
screens.body: He adds up each category for the week.

q.hint: A subscription charges the same amount on repeat, usually monthly.
q.explanation: The streaming charge repeats each month, so it's a subscription. These are worth reviewing a few times a year.

q.prompt: Sort Noah's next transactions into categories.
q.hint: Bills arrive whether you choose them or not. Eating out is a choice each time.
q.explanation: Power and phone are regular bills; brunch and delivery belong in eating out.

q.prompt: Noah also had a $18.50 café brunch. With the $41.90 food delivery, what did he spend on **eating out** this week?
Match each tracking method to what it's best at.
q.explanation: Apps save effort, spreadsheets give control, and envelopes stop you spending past a limit.

q.prompt: Noah budgeted $400 for eating out this month. His tracking shows he spent $530. By how much did he go over?
q.explanation: $530 − $400 = $130 over. He can trim next month or move money from another category.

q.prompt: Four weekly grocery shops: $92.30, $88.10, $105.60 and $79.00. What's the monthly grocery total?
q.explanation: The four shops add up to $365.00 for the month.

q.prompt: Noah's groceries come in $60 under budget but eating out is $130 over. Using his zero-based budget, what's the best next step?

options.text: Move the $60 to eating out and plan to trim the other $70 next month
Stop tracking, since budgets don't work for him
options.why: Going over once is normal. Tracking is what showed him where to adjust.

options.text: Ignore it: it all evens out
options.why: Overspends that aren't noticed tend to repeat.

q.explanation: Budgets are meant to be adjusted. Moving money between categories keeps every dollar assigned.

screens.title: Your 10-minute audit
screens.body: Open your banking app and scroll through last month. Total two categories: eating out and subscriptions. Anything surprising?
screens.action: Total last month's **eating out** and **subscriptions** from your bank app.

bullets: Tracking shows what you really spend; it beats guessing.
Use 6 to 8 categories that match your budget.
Compare plan with actual monthly and adjust, without guilt.

reviewBank.prompt: You budgeted $250 for transport and spent $210. How much under budget are you?

options.why: Spreadsheets suit some people; others never open them.
Free tools like your banking app work fine.

reviewBank.explanation: Consistency beats features. A simple method you keep up with wins.
Fuel and fares are transport; supermarket and market trips are groceries.

reviewBank.prompt: Small, repeated purchases are the easiest spending to forget.
reviewBank.explanation: Big bills stick in memory; little repeats slip by. Tracking catches them.
